name: Scientific research and development

scores.reads_as: A laboratory microscope: tilted body tube, curved arm, short stage and a wide base. A finance user would read it as science or lab work, and therefore R&D.
problems: At 16px the tilted tube shrinks to a small rounded blob. The eyepiece and objective can't be told apart, so the tube only reads as a microscope because of the arm and base around it.

The two stacked horizontal lines at the bottom (stage and base) look like an equals sign at 16px. They also resemble the double underline used on the securitisation icons (rmbs, cmbs, abs, clo), but the uneven lengths keep them apart well enough.

The solid style changes only the tube, which becomes a filled block. The arm and base stay as strokes, so the solid icon looks lighter than solid icons with large fills, such as professional-services. This is acceptable and in line with crops and agriculture.
The joint between tube and arm is a tiny notch. At 20 and 24px it nearly disappears, so the tube can look like it is floating on the arm rather than attached to it.
fixes: Optional: at 16px, add a 1px gap or step between the eyepiece and the main tube so the tube looks less like a blob.
Optional: make the stage line clearly shorter at 16 and 20px, or move it up 1px, so the bottom doesn't look like an equals sign or the securitisation underline.
Optional: at 20 and 24px, make the tube clearly touch or overlap the arm's arc so the joint reads as solid.

why: ISIC 72 and NACE 72 currently borrow the briefcase from professional services. Microscope is visibly distinct from the flask, DNA and briefcase icons.

name: Gambling and betting activities

scores.reads_as: A tilted die (five face at 24–48px, three face at 16–20px), which anyone would read as gambling or betting.
problems: The face changes across sizes: 16 and 20px show three pips, 24/32/48px show five. This is a sensible simplification, but users will see it when the sizes sit side by side.
At 24px the five pips are small and tight against the rotated outline, especially in the solid version, where the knockout dots are close to the minimum readable size.
The die is rotated about 15°, so the outline edges do not sit on the pixel grid and look slightly soft at 16px compared with the axis-aligned icons nearby (minor).
The die has a slightly larger optical footprint than the parent mask at 48px. This is within tolerance.
fixes: Optional: at 24px, enlarge the pips slightly (about 0.25px radius) or pull them in a little from the corners so the solid knockouts have more room.
Optional: consider using the three-pip face at 24px too, so the pip pattern is the same across more sizes. Keep five pips for 32/48px.

why: ISIC 92 and NACE 92 currently borrow the theatre mask from arts-recreation. A die is a clear, simple drawable object and is distinct from every existing icon.

scores.reads_as: A small, uneven server stack with an 'open in new / external link' arrow. It reads as 'export server' or 'send to server', not as rising spending on infrastructure.
problems: The plain 45° up-right arrow is the standard 'external link / open in new' glyph, not a trend. With nothing to show it is a rise in spending, it reads as a navigation action.

The server metaphor is broken. The top rack unit is full width, but the bottom one is shrunk to a small square to make room for the arrow. Two units of different widths don't read as a rack, and the bottom one looks like a checkbox or toggle.

At 16px the bottom unit's slot line is gone and only a dot is left. In solid at 16 and 20 it becomes a small blob with a dot. The detail changes from size to size, and the lower half looks like a radio button.
The bottom-right corner is crowded. At 16 and 20 the arrow sits nearly against the small unit, and the gap between them clogs, especially in solid.

The footprint is wide and short. Both units together fill only the middle band of the frame, while neighbours such as gambling-betting, cmbs and loans use the full height. In the per-size preview it looks lighter and smaller than the set at 16 and 20.
There's no link to money or spend. 'Spending' rests entirely on an ambiguous arrow.
The near/sibling preview only showed this icon again, so the check against its parent and siblings couldn't be done visually. Distinctness was judged from the sheets only.
fixes: Keep a proper server stack: two or three rack units of the same width, each with a slot line and an LED dot, filling about 70% of the frame height on the left or bottom.

Replace the bare diagonal arrow with an uptrend polyline: a zig-zag line with an arrowhead, taken from the existing uptrend metaphor in data/metaphors.json. Run it up and across the top-right corner, or rising out of the top of the stack, so it reads as growth and not as an external link.
Alternatively, put the stack inside the frame and add a small rising bar trio or trend line beside it. Don't shrink a rack unit to make room.
At 16 and 20px, draw a separate simplified version: two full-width units, a dot in each, no slot lines, and at least 1.5px clear space between the stack and the trend arrow.
For solid, knock the LED dots and slot lines out of filled units and keep the trend line as a stroke, so the footprint matches the outline and the lower unit doesn't collapse into a blob.
Scale the composition up to use the full 2px-inset live area at every size, so the visual weight matches neighbours like loans and cmbs.

scores.reads_as: A low ribbed box with a price tag on its top-right corner. At 32–48px it reads as a shipping container with a price tag. At 16–24px it reads more like a barcode, battery or product with a price tag, which suggests retail pricing or a sale rather than tariffs or trade.
problems: The container is a flat, wide strip, about 2:1, using only the bottom ~55% of the frame. The top-left quadrant is empty, so the icon looks bottom-heavy and sits smaller than neighbours like rmbs, cmbs and packaging, which fill the full height.

The container has no container cues: no top or bottom rails, corner posts or door end. Four bars in a rounded rectangle read as a barcode or battery, so the tag reads as a retail price tag (pricing or a sale) rather than a customs duty.
At 16px the ribs shrink to 3 short stubs crowded against the left wall, and the tag's punch hole is a ~1px speck that almost closes up.
In solid at 16 and 20px the tag merges into the container's top-right corner with no clear knockout gap, so they become one blob. The tag stops reading as a separate object.

The near-siblings preview (agent-tariffs-trade-near.png) is identical to the size sheet. It shows no parent or sibling icons, so distinctness against the parent theme could not be checked in context. Against the full sheet it is distinct (marine-shipping and packaging differ).
fixes: Make the container taller, about 3:2: at 24px roughly x3–19, y8–20. Let the tag overlap the container's top-right more and extend to y≈2–3, so the pair fills the 24px live area in both directions like its neighbours.

Add container cues: a top and bottom rail (inset horizontal lines or a thicker frame band), or corner-post verticals at both ends. Use 3–4 evenly spaced corrugation ribs that run nearly the full inner height, so it reads as a shipping container, not a barcode or battery.
At 16px, draw 2–3 ribs with at least 2px clear between them and the walls. Make the tag hole at least 2px across or replace it with a notch. At 20px use 3 ribs.

In solid, cut a knockout gap of at least 1px (1.5px at 24) between the tag and the container body at every size. Keep the tag hole as a clear knockout, so the tag stays a separate shape at 16 and 20px.
Check that the outline and solid bounding boxes match after the resize, and rerender the near-siblings preview with the actual parent and sibling icons.
